country.comment: The study examines urban water provision in Kampala, Uganda (with minor national-level Ugandan urban water context and brief mention of Rakai and Jinja in Uganda).

effect_estimate.comment: Descriptive administrative/historical statistics and qualitative case-study findings; no inferential econometric effect estimate is reported. Note a minor internal discrepancy in the authors' comparison of pre-paid vs vendor prices: p. 12 states ~17 UGX per 20L jerry-can is 'roughly a third' of vendor prices, while p. 14 states it is 'about five times lower'.
effect_estimate.value: Descriptive statistics and qualitative case findings — no inferential statistical effect estimate reported. Key empirical findings: (1) Although overall Kampala water supply coverage rose from 48% (1998) to 73%, 60% of Kampala's ~1.6 million residents live in informal settlements where lack of municipal planning and unclear property/tenure rights block private piped connections; in 2007, only ~6,000 of 170,000 urban water connections nationwide were in poor urban areas. (2) Standpipes generated <1% of Kampala water revenue in 1931–1948 (~7% of water supplied in 1968); in 2006, standpipes/kiosks across NWSC towns (3,122 built in 2002–2009) accounted for 4.7% of water sold and 2.1% of revenue, and despite a kiosk bulk tariff set at 65% of private connection tariffs, vendor markups caused poor residents to pay 4 to 8 times domestic connection prices. (3) NWSC's 2004 connection policy (subsidizing installation up to 50 m) doubled monthly new connections after one year (>20,000 new connections/year nationally) but raised tariffs by an average of 10%, leading to arrears, debt accumulation, and widespread disconnections of poor households, vendor standpipes, and 2006 politically pledged 'yellow water' taps. (4) Institutionalizing pro-poor targets under Internally Delegated Area Management Contracts (IDAMCs), opening a dedicated Kisenyi pro-poor branch (>100,000 residents), and installing ~390 pre-paid electronic water meters by 2009 with an approved pro-poor tariff (~17 UGX per 20-litre jerry-can, roughly one-third to one-fifth of local vendor prices) cut out vendor markups, but removed informal vendor credit and faced obstruction from landlords forcing tenants to buy higher-priced water from them rather than sign up for pre-paid meters.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF pp. 4-5, Section 'The colonial legacy'; PDF pp. 6-13, Section 'Public service provision and the urban poor'; PDF p. 14, Section 'Discussion and conclusions'

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped at 2 by non-experimental/non-quasi-experimental design. Assigned 2 because the study directly documents how specific legal, tenure, planning, tariff/connection-subsidy, contractual (IDAMC), disconnection, and landlord/vendor mechanisms operate on urban poor water access in Kampala through archival records, NWSC operational data, and primary fieldwork in Kisenyi I and II.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 3-14, main text; PDF pp. 15-17, Notes 4-78

mechanism_flags.comment: Covers colonial and informal land tenure/landlord-tenant barriers (tenure), unclear land ownership/property rights (property), municipal physical planning requirements (planning), colonial township/Kibuga split and decentralized branch service areas (service_area), connection subsidies, tariff increases, vendor markups, and pre-paid tariffs/token replacement charges (fees), pro-poor pilot branch/pre-paid tariff/50m subsidy adaptations (accommodation), door-to-door outreach and one-stop-shop branch assistance (bureaucratic_assistance), parish committees, local caretakers, and toilet user committees (participation), IDAMC contractual governance vs presidential campaign 'yellow water' patronage (political_coordination), and disconnections for non-payment/arrears (disconnection).
mechanism_flags.value: ELIGIBILITY, BURDEN, DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, ENFORCEMENT, tenure, property, planning, service_area, fees, accommodation, bureaucratic_assistance, participation, political_coordination, disconnection
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 3-14, Sections 'A century of water supply in Kampala', 'Public service provision and the urban poor', and 'Discussion and conclusions'

outcome_flags.comment: Examines private/yard-tap/pre-paid connections (formal_connection), access to safe public water in informal settlements (water_access), public toilets/latrines in informal settlements and the Kisenyi pilot (sanitation_access), citywide vs slum coverage rates (service_coverage), tariff/vendor/pre-paid water prices and ability to pay (affordability), disconnections and standpipe closures for non-payment (service_continuity), and low per-capita consumption of 0-20 L/capita/day in poor settlements (service_quantity).
outcome_flags.value: formal_connection, water_access, sanitation_access, service_coverage, affordability, service_continuity, service_quantity
outcome_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 6-14, Sections 'Public service provision and the urban poor' and 'Discussion and conclusions'

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Selected Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework because the paper is framed and structured as an institutional-historical / historical-geographical study (1890-2010) without a formal social-science Methods section, synthesizing colonial archival records, statutory/contractual instruments, utility administrative reports, and endnote-cited field interviews in Kisenyi I and II (if evaluated solely on the 2006/2008 parish fieldwork component, CASP Qualitative Checklist would be the closest conventional alternative).
risk_of_bias_tool.where_found: PDF pp. 2-3, Abstract and Introduction; PDF pp. 15-17, Notes 4-78

sample_size.comment: The article has no formal methods section in the main text; Note 61 reports empirical fieldwork in 2 parishes (Kisenyi I and Kisenyi II) including interviews with 30 standpost water vendors (21 female, 9 male) and unspecified numbers of community leaders, utility officials, project consultants, and NGO representatives (individual interviews also cited in Notes 48, 54, 63, 67, 68, 71, 72, 74, 78), alongside archival and policy documents (1913-2010) covering Kampala's ~1.6 million residents (>100,000 in the pilot parishes).
sample_size.value: 2 case study parishes in Kampala (Kisenyi I and Kisenyi II); 30 water vendors interviewed (21 female, 9 male) plus unspecified numbers of elected community leaders, public utility officials, project consultants, and NGO representatives
sample_size.where_found: PDF p. 11, Section 'The return of the coin-in-the-slot machine'; PDF pp. 15-17, Acknowledgements and Notes 48, 54, 61, 63, 67, 68, 71, 72, 74, 78

study_design.comment: Described by the authors as a 'historical geography' taking a 'historical and geographical approach'; operationalized via colonial archival sources (UK and Kenya National Archives), Uganda water sector statutes, performance contracts, and NWSC reports, combined with primary qualitative interviews in two Kampala parishes in 2006 and 2008 documented in the endnotes.
study_design.value: Historical-geographical and institutional case study combining archival research, policy/utility document analysis, and primary qualitative interviews
study_design.where_found: PDF pp. 2-3, Title, Abstract, and Introduction; PDF pp. 15-17, Notes 4-78

evidence_quotes.page: PDF p. 6, Section 'Spatial structure of informality'
evidence_quotes.quote: Informal settlements have not been considered to meet the minimum municipal planning requirements for installations of public water and sewerage infrastructure. Typically, informal settlements are characterised by a lack of physical planning, unclear land ownership and low incomes.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF p. 8, Section 'Spatial structure of informality'
evidence_quotes.quote: In 2007, out of a total of 170,000 water connections in all Ugandan towns only around 6000 are found within poor urban areas.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF p. 9, Section 'Current service provision for the poor'
evidence_quotes.quote: While the connection cost has been lowered, the cost of water has on the contrary increased as a result of the new policy; in order to cover the increased workload and costs of the utility, the water tariff has been increased by an average of 10%.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF p. 9, Section 'Current service provision for the poor'
evidence_quotes.quote: Many vendors are failing to pay their bills in time, and this is leading to debt accumulation, and consequently massive disconnections of public standpipes.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF p. 13, Section 'Water for the urban poor: the magic bullet?'
evidence_quotes.quote: A challenge to the project is also that some of the landlords in the project area are reportedly forcing their tenants to buy water at a higher cost from them, thus denying them the ability to sign up for a pre-paid meter.
Of the vendors, a majority, 21, were female, and the remaining nine were male.
